paras: The lynching of John Taylor and J. T. Bruce took place on the night of Saturday, September 10, 1881, at Dardanelle, Yell County, Arkansas, when an armed mob took the two men, both charged with murder, from the town jail and hanged them from a tree nearby. A Little Rock dispatch carried the story nationally and said public opinion was with the lynchers, while an Arkansas weekly condemned the act and blamed slow courts for it.

According to a Memphis Appeal special, Bruce had quarreled the previous winter with a young man named White near Dardanelle, then met him on the road, seized him by the hair and cut his throat; the dispatch added that Taylor "murdered White while claiming to be an officer." The Chicago Tribune's correspondent wrote that the prisoners' lives had been "repeatedly threatened" and that they had been moved from place to place. On the Thursday night before the lynching, the Yell County sheriff, warned that a mob meant to break into the Danville jail, chained Taylor, Bruce and a third prisoner, W. F. Burris, together and hid them in the woods until daylight while the mob searched for them. Taylor and Bruce were then placed in the jail at Dardanelle, and Burris was taken to Dover on a change of venue to Pope County.

On Saturday night armed, mounted men rode into Dardanelle and surrounded the jail; most reports put them at about one hundred, the Superior Times at two hundred, and the Columbia Banner described them as masked. According to the Chicago Tribune, they overpowered the guards, took the keys, removed Taylor and Bruce from an iron cage and put ropes around their necks. Townspeople woken by the commotion gathered but "could do nothing, as tho mob was desperate and determined."

The prisoners were dragged through the streets to a patch of timber at the edge of town and hanged from the limb of a tree. Spectators quoted in the dispatch said both men were nearly lifeless before they reached the tree and died cursing their executioners after "a desperate struggle." The mob then dispersed quietly.

Burris escaped because he was in the Dover jail, although the Memphis Appeal reported a rumor that he would be lynched on September 12. The Russellville Democrat said that, by rumor, the mob included some of "the very best and heretofore law abiding citizens of Yell county." The Savannah Morning News reported "intense excitement in Yell and adjacent counties," but no report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage.

The story first ran on September 13 as a Little Rock dispatch, at length in the Chicago Tribune and briefly in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier, and on September 14 it appeared in New York, Savannah, St. Paul, Portland and Eureka papers, with weekly summaries repeating it through September 24. Headlines such as "Judge Lynch" and "Two Murderers Hung" called the men murderers rather than accused prisoners. The wire said such lynchings were "becoming common in this section" and that public opinion favored them owing to loose justice in the courts; the St. Paul Daily Globe headlined it "Arkansas Lynchers Justified." The Chillicothe Crisis in Missouri said the men were lynched because they were "likely to escape justice by changes of venue."

The Russellville Democrat called the lynching "a terrible precedent" deserving "the condemnation of all good law abiding citizens," but in the same paragraph blamed court delays, technicalities, pardons and jail escapes for it. A week later its editorial "Mob Law" regretted "the growing popularity of Judge Lynch in our State" yet treated the lynchings as an attestation of the public demand that crime be punished. None of the reports stated the race of Taylor, Bruce or the members of the mob.

Two New England briefs named the lynched men "Taylor and White," but the Memphis Appeal identified White as the man Bruce was accused of killing, and all other reports named Bruce. Bruce's initials appear as "J. T." in most reports and "J. F." in the Chillicothe Crisis.
